summary: Annisquam Harbor Light, Gloucester, Massachusetts: a light since 1801, a brick tower of 1897, Life-Saving Service rescues in 1884 and 1888, and automation in 1974.

lens.where: Fifth-order lens (1857) replaced by a fourth-order lens in 1922 (NRHP). The current optic is a VRB-25 (USLHS).

structures.note: Cylindrical brick tower, 41 feet, on the stone foundations of the 1801 tower (NRHP; LighthouseFriends).
Altered in 1897 and renovated in 1984; occupied by a Coast Guard family (NRHP; LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Coast Guard property. Grounds, dwelling and tower closed. Directions run through the private Norwood Heights development.

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard (owner; retains the tower and 1.3 acres)

events.note: Act of Congress (29 April 1800) authorizes a light on Wigwam Point; Gustavus Griffin sells 6.5 acres in October 1800 for $140
Wooden octagonal tower (about 32 ft, $2,000) and two-room keeper's dwelling built
Fixed white light 40 feet above the water
Civil Engineer I. W. P. Lewis inspects; recommends the whole establishment be rebuilt
New white octagonal 40-foot tower in place; keeper's dwelling repaired
Fifth-order Fresnel lens, turned by clockwork
Covered walkway (109 ft) to the tower built (LighthouseFriends). The nomination dates a 75-foot walk to 1814; not resolved.
Three men from a wreck on Coffin's Beach landed by the Annisquam keeper with a Humane Society boat; the Davis Neck station was closed for the summer
Coal-laden schooner driven ashore on Coffin's Beach in a northeast gale, 26 September 1888 (name printed differently in the two sources)
Six men and the captain's wife rescued by volunteers with the Humane Society surf-boat kept at the Annisquam light
Keeper John W. Davis capsizes in a dory while collecting driftwood; rescued by fishermen and the Life-Saving crew (May 1895, LighthouseFriends)
Present brick tower (41 ft) built on the stone foundations of the previous tower
Fifth-order light moved to a temporary tower on 23 April 1897; re-established in the new tower on 13 July 1897
Color of the tower changed 16 October 1899; the report does not say to what
Fourth-order lens installed in place of the fifth-order lens; light source changed from oil to electricity
Fog horn established (LighthouseFriends); the nomination's chronology shows a fog signal by 1965
Light completely automated; last keeper relieved
Coast Guard deeds 4.9 acres to the Norwood Heights Trust with an easement for access; keeps 1.3 acres
Brick tower repaired (about 3,000 bricks), rusted landing beams and the 1801 keeper's house roof replaced; completed August 2000

wrecks.vessel: coal-laden schooner (name printed as 'Abbie P. Cranmer' in the Life-Saving Service report; 'Abbie B. Cramer' in LighthouseFriends)
wrecks.outcome: Driven ashore on Coffin's Beach; six men and the captain's wife rescued. Sources differ on the wreck's fate: the Life-Saving Service says it broke up two months later; LighthouseFriends says a complete loss.

keepers.name: Mary Phipps
keepers.note: Listed as principal keeper for 1871 in both the Digital Archive and LighthouseFriends; neither describes her further.

keepers.name: Sherman
keepers.note: The archive gives only the surname 'Sherman' with a span beginning in the 1950s.

corrections.why: The 1801 tower was replaced by the present brick tower in 1897; the record's 'built 1801' belongs to the first tower.
The nomination and the USLHS record both describe a cylindrical tower, not a conical one.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The first light (1801, wooden octagonal tower) and the present brick tower (1897) are different structures, as the nomination, LighthouseFriends and the USLHS record agree.

notes_for_editor: CHECKED 2026-10-22 (fact-check). (1) Walkway: the nomination dates a 75-foot wood walk to 1814 ($1,000) and says it was replaced in kind in 1978; LighthouseFriends dates a covered 109-foot walkway to 1867. A walk existed by 1842 (Day's 1843 statement). Both dates are reported; not resolved. (2) The 1888 wreck: the Life-Saving Service text (FY1888 report, scan p. 123) gives the schooner as 'Abbie P. Cranmer'; LighthouseFriends gives 'Abbie B. Cramer'. The story gives no name. Boat distance: three-quarters of a mile (LSS) vs two miles carried (LighthouseFriends); both are now stated. Fate: broke up two months later (LSS) vs complete loss (LighthouseFriends); both are reported. (3) The 1895 capsizing is from LighthouseFriends. The Life-Saving Service's 1895 services table (scan 174, printed 169) appears to have an entry for an overturned boat with the Annisquam keeper aboard, but its columns run together in the OCR, so it was not matched by position and is not cited. (4) Fog signal: LighthouseFriends dates the first fog horn to 1931; the nomination's chronology says the fog signal had been installed by 1965, and its 1981 text calls the present signal 'recently added'. Reported as a conflict. (5) Characteristic: the 1981 nomination describes a 10.4-rpm sector light with red and black sectors; the record says Fl W 7.5s. Not used in the story; the record's value is not checked. (6) Height in 1801: LighthouseFriends says a 32-foot tower; the nomination's 1800 map plan gives 40 feet of woodwork. The story gives only the 40-foot height of the light above the water (LighthouseFriends). (7) The 1851 tower and 1857 lens are from LighthouseFriends only. (8) Living persons: LighthouseFriends' keeper list includes Francis S. Davis (1963 to at least 1964), not on the Digital Archive roster; not added. Later keepers on the roster (Pittsley, Houde, Tuggle, Deo) appear by name only in the record; the story does not name them. LighthouseFriends' anecdote about a keeper's insurance advertisement is not used. (9) The 1843 statement by George Day is quoted through LighthouseFriends, which prints it from Lewis's 1843 report to Congress. The Congressional text was not read (loc.gov is not read directly). (10) The 1901 Board entry on dwelling repairs was located but its page was not confirmed; not cited. (11) Edward Hooper's letter (the cows, the 1888 account) is known through LighthouseFriends; the letter itself was not read. (12) The NRHP listing date (1987, per the record) is not stated in the story. (13) LighthouseFriends' parking-lot closure (2012) and its visitor directions are from a visitor report; the story attributes the claim to LighthouseFriends. (14) The 1972 vs 1980 disposal of the 4.9 acres is a conflict inside the nomination itself: its chronology gives 1980 and a note in its description gives 1972. Both are stated in the story. (15) The roster line 'Mary Phipps (1871-1871)' is the only female first name among the principal keepers; the archive does not give sex, so the story says 'the only woman's name'.
